title: §.VII: Opponents nearly αὐτοκατάκριτοι — they stretch the Invariata to swallow the Formula, then Dorsche's own canons clear the Philippica
pass_a_gloss: Finally they are found at odds with themselves and all but αὐτοκατάκριτοι, who either (1.) so enlarge the unvaried Augsburg Confession and its Sense that they even say the domestic Doctrines of the Formula of Concord alone — e.g. on the Oral Manducation of the Body of Christ, on the Ubiquity or Omnipresence of the Body of Christ, and the like (of which the Augsburg Confession never even dreamed) — yes, the whole Formula of Concord is comprehended in it, yet with the Philippica Confession, varying in some points, struck out, so as to make room for Brentian interpretations and Consequences, Melanchthonian ones being forbidden and shut out. Where the finger of the otherwise most learned of Lutheran Theologians, and not to be named by me except with veneration, Johann Georg Dorsche, points in his Secular Disputation on the more noted Consequences of the Augsburg Confession, forming among others these Conclusions: The Interpretation of the Augsburg Confession admits whatever has been deduced from it by legitimate Consequence. Also: The Religion of the Augsburg Confession is not to be so narrowed by interpreting that it must be said to be expressed totally and according to all its Articles in the Augsburg Confession (ch. 2, pp. 182 and 200). To wit: Whatever the Formulists have already invented or will invent hereafter will have been the Doctrine of the unvaried Augsburg Confession, inasmuch as deduced from it by legitimate consequence (as it seems to them); whatever on the contrary Philip — for declaring the Augsburg Confession once framed by himself (whose best interpreter, as of his own words, he can therefore seem) — either added or changed, and what the Philippists Pezel, Sohn, Crocius, Georg Pauli, Hoffmann, the Helmstedt men, and others also comment on the Augsburg Confession and deduce thence by consequences that seem legitimate to them, that is to be held most alien from the unvaried Augsburg Confession. Or (2.) with the same Dorsche in the following third chapter they forge Canons of that sort which, as not straying from the truth and therefore admitted, show the Varied Philippica Confession altogether genuine to all who weigh it with an equal balance, and only odiously harassed even by Dorsche. Variation of the Augsburg Confession of whatever kind, says Dorsche, even Substantial, ought not to have persuaded anyone to a passage to another religion (Canon 2). Therefore he who adheres to the Philippica Confession, though substantially varied according to Dorsche, still adheres to that Religion which the unvaried Augsburg Confession professes, and the Philippica Confession does not persuade a passage to another Religion than this, still less binds the same man to another Religion. Again: Variation, says Dorsche, that brings no change into the Substance of Truth set out in the Articles of the Augsburg Confession ought not to be odiously harassed or to be a cause of setting anyone outside the peace of Religion (Canon 3). Also: Variation that leaves their place to the Original exemplars does not stand in the way of the sincerity of the Augsburg Confession (pp. 216, 217, 218). I subsume concerning the Variata Philippica: this does not bring a change into the Substance of Truth [Mentzer bearing witness], but leaves their place to the Original Exemplars, if any still survive anywhere. Therefore.
pass_b_english: Finally these opponents are caught at odds with themselves — all but αὐτοκατάκριτοι.

(1.) They stretch the unvaried Augsburg Confession and its sense so wide that they even fold into it the Formula of Concord's household doctrines — oral manducation of Christ's body, ubiquity or omnipresence of Christ's body, and the like — of which the Augsburg Confession never so much as dreamed — yes, the whole Formula, they say, is packed inside it.
Yet they strike out the Philippica Confession where it varies in some points, so as to make room for Brentian readings and consequences while Melanchthon's are barred and shut out.

Where the finger of Johann Georg Dorsche points — otherwise among the most learned Lutheran divines, and a name I speak only with reverence — in his Secular Disputation on the more noted consequences of the Augsburg Confession, forming among others these conclusions:
Interpretation of the Augsburg Confession admits whatever is drawn from it by legitimate consequence.
Also: Augsburg religion is not to be so narrowed by interpreting that it must be said to be expressed wholly, and in all its articles, inside the Augsburg Confession itself (ch. 2, pp. 182 and 200).
In plain: whatever the Formulists have already spun, or will invent later, is to count as unvaried Augsburg doctrine — because deduced, as they see it, by legitimate consequence.

But whatever Philip added or changed in declaring the Confession he himself once framed — and he may well seem its best interpreter, as of his own words — and whatever Philippists (Pezel, Sohn, Crocius, Georg Pauli, Hoffmann, the Helmstedt men, and others) comment and draw by consequences that seem legitimate to them, that is to be held most alien from the unvaried Confession.

(2.) Or with the same Dorsche in the next, third chapter they mint canons which, if admitted as not far from the truth, show the Variata Philippica altogether genuine to anyone who weighs it with an even hand — and only odiously harassed, even by Dorsche.
Variation of the Augsburg Confession of whatever kind, says Dorsche, even substantial, ought not to have talked anyone into crossing to another religion (Canon 2).

Therefore he who holds to the Philippica, though Dorsche calls it substantially varied, still holds to the religion the unvaried Augsburg Confession professes; the Philippica does not urge a crossing to another religion, still less binds a man to one.
Again: variation that brings no change into the substance of truth set out in the Augsburg articles ought not to be odiously harassed or used to push anyone outside the peace of religion (Canon 3).
Also: variation that leaves the original exemplars their place does not block the sincerity of the Augsburg Confession (pp. 216–218).
I subsume for the Variata Philippica: it brings no change into the substance of truth — Mentzer is witness — and it leaves the original exemplars their place, if any still survive. Therefore.
source_text: Denique sibi ipsis adversi & tantum non αὐτοκατάκριτοι deprehenduntur, qui vel (1.) Confessionem Augustanam invariatam hujusque Sensum adeò ampliatum eunt, ut etiam soli Formulae Concordiae domesticas Doctrinas, e.g. de Orali Corporis Christi Manducatione, de Ubiquitate seu Omnipraesentia Corporis Christi, similesque, (de quibus ne somniavit quidem Augustana Confessio) quin totam Concordiae Formulam illacomprehenfam ajunt, expunctâ tamen variante in nonnullis, Philippicâ Confessione, Brentianis sic interpretationibus & Consequentibus locum facturi, prohibitis exclusisque Melanchthonianis. Quorsum digitum intendit doctissimus alioquin Lutheranorum Theologorum & non nisi cum veneratione mihi nominandus, Joh. Georg. Dorscheus, Disp. Seculari de Consequentibus Augustanae Confessionis insignioribus, quippe has inter alias, Conclusiones formans: Interpretatio Augustanae Confessionis admittit, quicquid ex ea per legitimam Consequentiam deductum est. Item: Religio August. Confess. non ita interpretando coangustanda est, ut totaliter & secundum omnes suos Articulos, in August. Confess. expressa esse dicenda sit, Cap. 2. pag. m. 182. & 200. Scilicet: Quicquid Formulistae vel jam commenti sunt, vel in posterum comminiscentur, istud August. Confess. invariatae Doctrina fuerit, quippe per legitimam consequentiam, (uti ipsis videtur,) ex ea deductum; Quicquid ex adverso, vel Philippus, declarandae ergo Augustanae Confess. à se ipso olim confectae (cujusque proinde interpres, ceu verborum suorum, optimus, videri potest) vel addidit, vel immutavit, Philipistae quoque Pezelius, Sohnius, Crocius, Georgius Pauli, Hoffmannus, Helmstadienses aliique commentantur in Augustanam Confessionem, perque legitimas sibi visas Consequentias inde deducunt, illud ab Augustana Conf. invariata quàm alienissimum habendum. Vel (2.) cum eodem Dorscheo, capite sequenti tertiô, Canones ejusmodi cudunt, qui, ceu à vero haud abludentes, indeque admissi, Variatam Confessionem Philippicam, omnibus aequâ istam lance expendentibus, omnino genuinam ostendunt, & nonnisi odiose, etiam à Dorscheo exagitatam. Variatio, inquit Dorscheus, Augustanae Confessionis quacunque, etiam Substantialis, non debuit alicui transitum ad aliam religionem suadere. Canon. 2. Ergò qui Philippicae adhaeret Confessioni, licèt substantialiter, juxta Dorscheum, variatae, adhuc dum Religioni illi adhaeret, quam Augustana Confessio invariata profitetur, nec Confessio Philippica ad aliam huic Religionem transitum suadet, nedum eundem alteri Religioni addicit. Iterum: Variatio, ait Dorscheus, in Substantiam Veritatis, Articulis Augustanae Confessionis expositae mutationem nullam inferens, non debet odiose exagitari aut causa esse aliquem extra pacem Religionis constituendi. Canon. 3. Item: Variatio, quae suum locum Originalibus exemplaribus relinquit, sinceritati Augustanae Confessionis, non obstat, p. m. 216. 217. 218. Subsumo ego: de Variata Philippica: Non infert haec mutationem in Substantiam Veritatis, [testante Mentzero] relinquit verò locum suum Originalibus Exemplaribus, si quae alicubi supersunt. Ergò.

lemmas.gloss: Melanchthon Variata vindicated by Dorsche canons
